title: Lesson 3: Addressing Issues Instead of Attacking Personalities
summary: Concentrate on the specific mistake and the expected improvement. Do not turn an operational problem into a judgment about someone's character.

items.label: Focus
items.body: Issue-focused communication, facts instead of labels, and practical solutions

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine a receptionist makes an error while recording a client's appointment.
The therapist assigned to the client discovers the mistake and says: "You're always so careless. I don't understand why you can't do simple things properly."
The receptionist becomes upset and responds: "You're not perfect either. You also make mistakes!"
The discussion turns into an argument about each person's character. Meanwhile, the original booking problem remains unresolved.
Now consider a different approach: "The appointment was recorded for 3 p.m., but the client confirmed 4 p.m. Let's correct the booking and agree on how to verify appointment times going forward."
This approach identifies the actual problem, corrects it and helps prevent recurrence.
The first approach attacks the person. The second addresses the issue.
At Zura Spa, employees should learn to separate operational problems from personal judgments.

sections.title: 2. What does addressing the issue mean?
paragraphs: Addressing the issue means concentrating on the specific action, mistake, misunderstanding or situation that requires attention.
It involves identifying what happened, understanding its effect and finding a practical solution.
For example: "The room wasn't ready before the appointment." This identifies a work-related problem.
By contrast: "You're lazy and irresponsible." This labels the employee's personality without explaining the precise issue.

sections.title: 3. Why personal attacks make conflict worse
paragraphs: Personal attacks often create additional problems beyond the original disagreement.
When employees feel personally attacked, they may concentrate on defending their dignity rather than understanding what needs improvement.
A workplace problem should not become a judgment about someone's entire character.
list: Distract attention from the actual issue.
Make employees afraid to report mistakes.

sections.title: 4. Focus on facts, not labels
paragraphs: The second column describes specific behaviours. This makes it easier to establish the facts and identify appropriate improvements.
table: "You interrupted me several times during the discussion."
"You arrived after your scheduled start time on three occasions."
"The instruction wasn't followed as discussed. Can we clarify it?"

sections.title: 5. Avoid exaggerations
paragraphs: Words such as always, never, everybody and nothing can make a disagreement more hostile, especially when they are inaccurate.
Unhelpful: "You never do anything properly."
Better: "The room checklist was incomplete after yesterday's session and again this morning."
Specific information is more useful than exaggerated criticism.

items.label: I — Identify the actual problem
items.body: Describe what happened without attacking the person.

items.label: S — Separate facts from assumptions
items.body: Confirm what is known and avoid guessing intentions.

items.label: U — Understand the other perspective
items.body: Allow relevant explanations and ask clarifying questions.

items.label: E — Establish a solution
items.body: Agree on what needs to change and who will take responsibility.

sections.title: 7. Practical example
paragraphs: Two therapists disagree about an unfinished room preparation.

Instead of arguing about who is lazy or irresponsible, they can discuss what preparation was required, which tasks were incomplete, who was assigned to complete them, whether there was a communication or handover problem, and what needs to happen before the next appointment.
If the responsibility remains disputed, the supervisor should clarify the arrangement.

sections.title: 8. When the issue involves repeated misconduct
paragraphs: Focusing on behaviour does not mean ignoring repeated problems.

If an employee repeatedly fails to complete assigned responsibilities, the supervisor may need to document the incidents, communicate expectations and follow the appropriate performance-management process.
The discussion should still remain factual and respectful.
Accountability and dignity can exist together.

sections.title: 9. Lesson 3 case study
paragraphs: A receptionist forgets to communicate an appointment change. The therapist responds by calling her incompetent in front of colleagues.
Expected lesson: Address the actual problem without making degrading judgments about the person involved.
list: What was the original operational problem?
Which statement turned the correction into a personal attack?
What should the therapist have said?
What responsibility belongs to the receptionist?
How can the booking process be improved?

sections.title: 10. Lesson 3 practical exercise
paragraphs: Rewrite the following statements as issue-focused feedback.
table: "The appointment was recorded incorrectly. Let's verify the details."
"This repeated handover issue is affecting the team, and we need to address it."
"The client's concern wasn't communicated promptly. Please ensure such concerns are escalated."

remember: When a problem occurs, focus on what happened, why it matters and what needs to change. Do not turn one mistake into a judgment about someone's entire personality.
